newsitem.title: ZAIRE: UN's Ogata visits refugees near Zaire war zone.
newsitem.headline: UN's Ogata visits refugees near Zaire war zone.

text.p: U.N. refugee chief Sadako Ogata on Saturday visited weak and frightened Rwandan Hutu refugees, trapped by Zaire's civil war in the village of Tingi Tingi on the edge of the combat zone.
Ogata, who is looking for ways of repatriating up to 300,000 Rwandan Hutus, went ahead with the visit despite earlier concerns for her security.
"The refugees have to move out. They have to go back but how, when and under what conditions, it's not clear," she told reporters.
Ogata went to Tingi Tingi from Kisangani, headquarters of Zaire's counter-offensive against Tutsi-led rebels in the east.
An estimated 120,000 Rwandan Hutus have been trapped by the war in Tingi Tingi after fleeing west from earlier fighting along the border with Rwanda and Burundi.
On the battle front, the governor of Maniema province and a senior military officer in the Tingi Tingi area said Amisi further down the road to the east had fallen to the rebels.
"The landing strip and the (refugee) camp are in the hands of the enemy," Governor Omari Sisi, whose province covers Amisi, told Reuters.
A senior army officer said rebels seized Amisi on Friday.
Both Zairean military officials and rebels report fighting at the gold and tin mining town of Punia, south of Lubutu, which is close to Tingi Tingi and 200 km (125 miles) from Kisangani.
Relief officials earlier reported refugees fleeing Amisi.
Ogata has discussed repatriation options with the government, whose forces are battling the Tutsi-led rebels for control of a string of towns on several fronts.

"The best way to evacuate the refugees is by road. I have heard that the refugees are prepared to walk back. Security corridors would be necessary and that's a political question," she said on Saturday.

In New York, the U.N. Security Council called for an end to hostilities, the withdrawal of all foreign forces from Zaire, including mercenaries, and demanded that combatants respect the rights of refugees.

The refugees and Hutu hardliners blamed for the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda fled west in December after attacks on their camps in the east. Many more fellow Hutus opted to return home, trekking en masse in the other direction.

Relief agencies pulled their international staff out of Tingi Tingi and Lubutu on Friday, saying panicky Zairean troops fired in the air and demanded money and vehicles from them. Aid workers said tension eased there later.
The rebels responded to the much-trumpeted January 20 government counter-offensive by attacking on several fronts.
Both sides have reported the fall or recapture of a handful of towns in the war zone, which stretches from a corner of the mineral-rich southern province of Shaba to the northeast.

Zaire, which accuses Rwanda and Uganda of invading in support of the rebels, said on Friday its army had retaken Watsa in the north east and Shabunda in the east. Officials said 800 rebels were killed and Ugandan soldiers taken prisoner at Watsa.

Veteran president Mobutu Sese Seko, meanwhile, returned to his Gbadolite jungle palace on Friday after medical tests in Europe. Mobutu, who had prostate surgery in August, denied asking Morocco for military help on a visit on his way home.
During the last six months Mobutu has spent only about three weeks in Zaire.
